That compares to $1.5 billion of funding for European startups in the defense space as of September a year earlier, based on the 2025 report.

In Europe, the segment of unmanned aerial vehicles accounted for $4.7 billion raised as of September, according to the Dealroom data, followed by Earth observation and satellite imagery with $1.8 billion, anti-drone solutions and launch vehicles, each with $1.2 billion, and maritime robotics, with $796 million raised.

Mega rounds made up more than 85% of the venture capital invested in European defense startups this year, including Helsing’s $1.8 billion Series E round in July according to Dealroom.
German startups have set every fundraising record in European defense-tech venture capital funding since 2023, the report said.
“Munich is the powerhouse of the European defense tech ecosystem,” Dealroom said. “Helsing and Quantum Systems drive most of it, together worth $25.7 billion.
Behind them a younger cohort is forming across ground robotics, counter-drone and hypersonics.”

items.title: Extreme Environments Push Chips To Their Breaking Point
items.originalTitle: Extreme Environments Push Chips To Their Breaking Point
items.summary: Orbital data centers, military/aerospace vehicles, HPC experiments, quantum, and advanced manufacturing equipment are all putting pressure on chips to withstand extreme environments. Chips that were once qualified against a limited set of operating conditions are now being designed for environments where multiple stresses hit at once. Radiation, thermal shock, vibration, pressure, noise, and cryogenic temperatures are colliding in applications ranging from orbital data centers and defense systems to particle physics, quantum computing, and advanced manufacturing.

evidenceRecords.text: Key Takeaways: Orbital data centers, military/aerospace vehicles, HPC experiments, quantum, and advanced manufacturing equipment are all putting pressure on chips to withstand extreme environments.
Chips that were once qualified against a limited set of operating conditions are now being designed for environments where multiple stresses hit at once.

For example, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) is working with Morgan State University, Northrop Grumman, and Project Omega on the DARPA-funded Rads to Watts program, which aims to convert Cold War-era radioactive decay into high-density nuclear micro-power radiovoltaic systems for extreme environments, including space, remote sensing, undersea infrastructure, and defense applications. [1] Radioisotopes such as Strontium-90 will be converted directly into electricity to operate for decades without refueling or battery replacement.
2: This illustrated setup shows how ASU’s extreme environments lab would test radiation and extreme cold together to mimic space.

items.summary: The incident is the latest suspected Russian drone incursion, as fears grow that the war in Ukraine could spill over. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has blamed a Russian drone attack for the sinking of a ship in Romania’s section of the Black Sea. Romania reported that two people were killed and 11 rescued when a grain ship caught fire and sank in its waters on Monday. The Ukrainian president’s claim suggests the incident is the latest in a series of suspected incursions along NATO’s eastern flank, and will fuel concerns that Moscow’s war in Ukraine could spill over.

items.title: Kraken and Saab team up for drone detection aboard uncrewed vessels
items.originalTitle: Kraken and Saab team up for drone detection aboard uncrewed vessels
items.summary: Kraken Technology Group and Saab UK have tested a prototype autonomous ‘drone seeker’ vessel for maritime environments. The experimental vessel combines Kraken’s K3 SCOUT uncrewed surface vessel with Saab UK’s Giraffe 1X radar designed to detect and track airborne threats in real time. Integrated into K3 SCOUT’s modular payload bay, Giraffe 1X is designed to provide early warning of aerial threats, detecting even small airborne targets at extended ranges. Kraken and Saab UK are both based in Fareham, where the K3 SCOUT and Giraffe 1X are manufactured.

evidenceRecords.text: Bright Factory is an intelligent manufacturing platform connecting design, automation, and data. | Source: Bright Machines Teradyne Inc. today announced a strategic investment in Bright Machines Inc., a builder of AI and data center infrastructure.
The companies are also launching a strategic collaboration focused on integrating Teradyne robotics and test technologies with Bright Machines’ manufacturing platform.

“Physical AI is changing what is possible on the factory floor, and Teradyne and Bright Machines are partnering to accelerate this evolution,” said Shantnu Sharma, chief development officer at Teradyne.

“The combination of Bright Machines’ depth in software-defined manufacturing and Teradyne’s decades of experience in robotics and test gives companies building AI infrastructure a faster path from design into production, with data behind every unit they build.” Teradyne and Bright Machines jointly automate production The partners said they plan to integrate Teradyne’s technologies into Bright Machines’ production environments.
At these sites, the Bright Machines manufacturing platform , Universal Robots’ force- and power-limited robots , and Teradyne’s board test systems would operate together on a production floor.

“By connecting these data streams with Bright Machines’ product genealogy and manufacturing intelligence capabilities, customers can maintain an end-to-end production data thread linking design decisions, assembly execution, and electrical performance,” asserted Teradyne.

“The next generation of AI infrastructure calls for a manufacturing approach that is more automated, software-defined, data-driven, and responsive to change,” stated Sviat Dulianinov, CEO of Bright Machines.

Their robotics and test technologies are complementary to our platform, and together we can help customers simplify integration, accelerate deployment, and maintain a complete production data thread.” Partners share AI infrastructure experience AI infrastructure is driving one of the largest electronics manufacturing buildouts in recent history, noted Teradyne.

Burlingame, Calif.-based Bright Machines brings a software-defined manufacturing platform spanning design, robotics, automation, inspection, material movement, production intelligence, and operations.
